(1) the brain is not an information processing machine, (2) it is an action processing machine that processes information to achieve its action goals, and (3) the action processing machinery is embodied in a physical system, and is not independent from the body, as it has always been thought.

a symbiotic robot is an autonomous system that learns from the human partner and from its own experiences how to interact with humans in a way that the interaction is mutually beneficial for both the human and the machine.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the design of a cognitive architecture which is able to support a robot in its interaction with a human partner, in a way which is not only functional but also socially acceptable, and in which the robot can learn from the interaction.
the development of the necessary cognitive mechanisms that may give symbiosis capabilities to collaborative robots.
the design and development of computational models of cognitive processes that can support the development of social skills for human robot symbiosis.

we are trying to build a "cognitive" robot that may interact with a human in a symbiotic way, in the sense that both partners may learn from each other, and that the robot may be able to understand what the human partner is doing, and to predict his/her future actions.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, if we are to build robots that can be our partners in symbiosis, we need to build a shared cognitive architecture that is able to support the development of a shared understanding of the world and of the actions of both human and robot.

the cognitive architecture for the next generations of collaborative robots must be designed in a totally different way from the conventional approaches: the brain of a symbiotic robot is a complex system of interacting cognitive processes, not a monolithic neural network.
the cognitive architecture for symbiotic robots must be a set of bi-directionally connected building blocks, not a monolithic hierarchical system.
